paper.title_en: The Price of Discovery: Cost-Optimized Detectors for the GUT-Scale QCD Axion
paper.abstract_en: Grand unification and string theory point to a quantum chromodynamics (QCD) axion with mass between $10^{-11}$ and $10^{-8}$ eV, while heterotic string theory suggests a mass of $0.5-0.8$ neV. We study which laboratory experiment could discover or exclude DFSZ-strength QCD axion dark matter at and above 0.5 neV at the lowest cost, which we estimate from scaling laws calibrated to historical data. We find that a lumped-element detector, building on the ABRACADABRA concept, can do so with demonstrated readout technology; an example is a shielded toroid about 14 m across with a 6 T NbTi magnet, whose magnet and cryostat we estimate at around 120 million Swiss francs (MCHF). If projected readout targets are met, a 5 m toroid at 25 MCHF suffices. We find these designs by optimizing the toroid, solenoid, and core lumped-element topologies under a common cost metric. The toroid emerges as the most promising and cost-effective topology. The optimal field of the toroid detector is far below the 16 T of the proposed DMRadio-GUT design, which would cost nearly twice as much as our optimum. Heterodyne searches with superconducting radio-frequency cavities, with cavity shapes that we optimize for price, cost between about the same as and twice as much as the lumped-element detectors, but require cavities of volumes $\sim50-2000$ m$^3$. We find that nuclear-magnetic-resonance searches (CASPEr) need orders-of-magnitude gains in spin polarization and coherence. We release axionMultiPhysics, an open-source finite-element and multiphysics package for, e.g., magnetoquasistatic and full-wave electromagnetics, superconductors, readout circuits, and mechanics, from which most of our numerical results were obtained.
